title: Practical Ways to Earn with ChatGPT

paragraphs.text: Before you begin
Adapted and expanded by Moses Afolabi • Illustrated edition • 2026

Five foundation chapters lead into five practical chapters containing two worked opportunities each: ten opportunities in total. Examples and results are fictional teaching material, not verified earnings or client testimonials.
Use public, fictional, or specifically authorized information for practice. Verify facts and protect client details. Tools, availability, and account controls change; check current official guidance.
OpenAI explains that ChatGPT can produce incorrect facts or invented references. Human checking remains essential. See OpenAI accuracy guidance and data-use controls.
This book promises no income and requires no particular paid plan. The PDF has still illustrations; its separate companion adds gentle motion.

Chapter 1 Find a problem worth solving
Ask about a specific difficulty before offering a paid solution.

A caterer may answer the same questions every Friday. An apartment manager may answer recurring move-in questions. A podcast host may spend an evening turning a new recording into an email. Each situation gives you a question to investigate. How often does this work come up, and what would a finished version save the person who has to do it?

Start with three conversations. Ask someone to describe the last time the task came up. Ask what information was missing and how they knew the job was done. An owner may say they want social media help, then tell you they spend most of their time responding to customers who cannot find the pickup address. The pickup problem gives you a smaller, clearer offer to test.

Use your first week to build evidence. On days one and two, choose a buyer and ask about their current process. On days three and four, describe a small paid outcome and produce a fictional sample. On day five, check the sample against your source notes and time yourself. On day six, show it to three relevant people. On day seven, write down which part they valued and whether anyone wanted to discuss a paid job.
Exercise. Complete these three sentences before opening ChatGPT.
My buyer spends time on ___ every ___.
I can deliver ___ using information the buyer can provide.
The buyer will know it works when ___.
If the final blank is hard to fill, show one person a draft and watch how they use it. Their first question often tells you what the finished work needs.
Compare two problems before choosing one

Suppose an appliance repair shop wants more social media posts and also loses time calling customers whose repair requests omit the appliance model or the problem. Ask the owner to describe both tasks. The posts may matter, but their effect is harder to measure in a short pilot. An intake form gives you a visible test. Hand it to someone unfamiliar with the shop and ask them to submit a realistic request. Count which questions the technician still needs to ask.

Work through the full path before quoting. The customer describes a problem, the technician reviews it, and someone confirms a drop-off. The form should collect useful facts at the start and leave diagnosis to the technician after inspection. An offer that promises a cleaner intake is something you can deliver and demonstrate.

Score each potential project from one to three on four questions. How easily can you contact the buyer? How often does the work recur? Can the buyer provide reliable source material? Can you show a noticeable improvement in one sample? Use the scores to choose your first conversation. A high score gets you to an interview. The buyer’s response tells you whether there is demand.
Make the unit of work clear

“I help local shops with AI” leaves the owner to imagine the project. “I make a repair intake form and three customer replies from your existing shop policies” gives the owner something to react to. Include the object you will deliver, the source they provide, and a boundary such as one location or one service. If they ask how fast you can start, determine who will approve the facts before you promise a date.

Investigate one recurring problem
Define a useful result
Test demand with a small offer
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Interview for a recent example

Ask, “When did this problem last interrupt your work?” A shop owner who says their booking system is confusing may describe several different troubles. One customer could miss an address. Another could miss a required deposit. A third could arrive when the shop is closed. Those problems have different causes and different fixes. Ask the owner to show you one recent instance using a redacted account or a fictional reconstruction. Write down the condition that created the problem and the action the staff member had to take.

Next ask, “Which part would pay for itself if it happened less often?” A small change in the booking message might be enough. An appointment form may need a clearer question. A rule the business has yet to decide needs an owner decision before anyone writes copy. Ask who can decide, when they will be available, and which existing document records the decision. Summarize what you understood in two or three sentences before offering a quote.

A useful interview output is a plain acceptance test. “A person who has never visited the building can identify the correct entrance from the confirmation email” is testable. “The email should feel more professional” invites an open-ended round of changes. You can still ask how formal the voice should be, but the test gives you a way to decide whether the work is usable.
Chapter 2 Build a sample and write the offer
Check draft claims against approved source material.

Imagine a caterer whose factual notes say orders usually require 48 hours of notice. A polished draft promises every customer that a 48-hour order will be accepted. That single change can create a promise the caterer cannot keep. A dependable answer explains the normal notice period and tells the customer how to confirm availability.

For your sample, use a fictional business with three straightforward policies and one deliberately ambiguous rule. Draft a short FAQ, then look for any answer that goes beyond the notes. A prospective customer should be able to see your judgment in the finished example.
Prompt to adapt

Use the approved policy notes below to draft five customer questions and answers. Answer each question directly, then give the next step. For missing facts, write “Confirm with owner” and add the exact question I need to ask. Include a table mapping each draft answer to the relevant source note.
Approved notes: [insert fictional or authorized notes]

Review the source mapping yourself. A plausible citation to the wrong policy can be as misleading as an invented policy. Verify dates, exceptions, prices and guarantees. Use fictional or specifically approved materials during drafting and keep private customer details out of sample work.

A simple offer. “I’ll turn your approved policies into ten customer FAQ answers and five reusable replies. You’ll receive an editable file, one revision round, and a version ready for your website or front-desk team.” Send a short invitation. “I made a sample showing how common pickup questions could be answered in one place. Would you like to see it? If it would help your team, I can quote a version based on your policies.” Send it to an appropriate prospect through a channel where a business inquiry is welcome. Let their response determine your next step.
Build the before and after

Imagine a salon’s appointment reminder reads, “See you soon. Let us know if anything changes.” A client still has to ask for the address and whether they can bring a guest. Ask the salon for its approved arrival instructions, guest policy, and cancellation procedure. Keep the intake to questions that affect the final message. If pricing varies by stylist, get the salon’s approved wording and link instead of estimating a price.

A strong after-sample uses a clear first sentence, a short arrival instruction, and a distinct next step. Put the original draft next to your revision and ask one test reader to find the address and identify how to reschedule. If they miss either, adjust the layout. A nicer sentence can help. A reader who can actually complete the task gives you stronger evidence.
Review the draft in two passes

First check substance. Confirm what each sentence promises, whether a condition disappeared, and who can approve an exception. Then check use. Read it on a phone, verify links, and test whether the shortest version still contains the essential information. Ask ChatGPT for a list of claims to verify against the approved notes. Check that list against the text yourself.

Before showing the sample, label invented business names, policies, and results as fictional. If someone wants to see previous client work, use only examples you have permission to share. A clear demonstration of your process can earn confidence before you have a portfolio.
Visual summary
Separate approved facts from drafts
Flag missing details
Verify the completed sample
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Make the pilot small enough to complete

A client asks for a handbook. A full handbook may require interviews, policy decisions and several approvals. Suggest a pilot with one task, such as processing a common return. Agree that the pilot covers the approved policy, a short procedure and one worked exception. Give the buyer a clear way to evaluate it. If a staff member can follow it and tell when to call a manager, the pilot has answered a real question about usefulness.
Before sending any work to ChatGPT, label your inputs by authority. A confirmed policy is a source. A customer complaint may point to a problem. A draft is a proposal. Ask

ChatGPT to preserve those differences and list contradictions for your review. If the confirmed process conflicts with what a supervisor said, return the question to the business. Resolving the discrepancy can be an important part of the project, but the decision belongs to the owner.

A pilot also clarifies whether the work is worth finishing. If the buyer declines the next phase, ask what prevented them from using the sample. It may need a simpler storage location or clearer ownership. Use the feedback to improve the next assignment. The knowledge becomes useful when it changes what you offer or how you deliver it.
Chapter 3 Price and deliver your first job
Agree on the deliverable, full workload, revisions, and acceptance test.

Price the work you will actually do. Give yourself time to interview the owner, untangle contradictory notes, check the draft, handle one revision, and package the files. For illustration, a 20-minute intake, 60 minutes of drafting, 45 minutes of checking, 35 minutes of revisions and 20 minutes of delivery total three hours. A $25 hourly target produces a $75 labor estimate before direct costs or fees. Treat those numbers as a worked example and replace them with your own.

Before beginning, confirm the deliverables, deadline, materials needed and revision limit in writing. Explain how you handle policy changes received after approval. When a five-question pilot becomes a request to rewrite the whole site, send an updated scope and price before undertaking the extra work.

Deliver the source of truth alongside the finished answers. For a FAQ, that can be a one-page record of the policy notes the buyer approved, the revision date and the person who confirmed the wording. Invite the buyer to test two answers with a staff member who normally takes calls. Ask whether the answers are easy to find and whether the next step is clear.

Worksheet. Estimate time for intake ___, drafting ___, checking ___, revisions ___, delivery ___. Record actual time after the job. If the difference came from unclear source material, add a short intake requirement to your next offer. If you spent an hour formatting, create a reusable document layout for your own use.
Quote with assumptions the customer can see

A retailer asks for ten product descriptions. Your initial estimate assumes each item has a fact sheet and the customer supplies all photos. During intake you discover that seven items have incomplete dimensions. Ask who can supply the missing numbers and whether the delivery date should begin after the facts arrive. Spell this out before quoting. Otherwise, chasing measurements may take longer than writing the copy.

Set one approval point. Send two representative listings before completing the rest. The owner can approve tone and structure while changes are still inexpensive. Once approved, write the remaining listings and mark any item that needs a fact checked. This gives the owner a clear way to review the project without reading a long email thread.
Deliver a handoff the client can use

Name files by purpose and date. Provide an editable file, the approved text in paste-ready form, and a short note showing who owns future updates. If a supplier changes a dimension after delivery, the client should know which description to change. Ask the owner to paste one listing into a draft page. Check whether the platform trims the title or removes formatting.

Write your own review after delivery. Compare estimated and actual time. Document which step you underpriced, then adjust the next quote or narrow the service. A job that took twice as long as planned can still teach you what to fix before you repeat it.
Price a revision before it becomes an argument

Suppose you quote an email sequence with approved copy and a single round of revisions. The client supplies a new service after approving the first version and asks you to include it throughout the sequence. Compare the request with the original scope. Check how many messages, offers and links would change. Give the client a clear option: keep the agreed delivery or approve an updated scope with a new price and date. Put the decision in writing before work begins. Protect the client from surprises as well. If a two-hour review has expanded because the files disagreed, explain what you found and ask whether the client wants you to reconcile them or whether the client can supply a definitive version. Keep work on the agreed deliverable moving where it can proceed. A question raised early gives both sides a choice. The same question raised on delivery day often gives neither side a useful option.

Time the first few assignments from intake to handoff. A provider who estimates only the drafting work can mistake revenue for useful profit. Record the time spent checking claims, arranging approval and packaging the files. If each project has an hour of cleaning because the buyer’s input arrives in five formats, design a short intake sheet. If the hour reflects necessary verification, include the work in your next quote.
Keep a project record people can review

Build a small delivery folder with the approved source, the editable final file and a short handoff note. A buyer should be able to open the note and see the delivery date, the approved version and the person who owns the next update. Mark open questions clearly. The buyer may want to publish only the part that is approved. Give them separate files or obvious labels for that purpose.

A useful verification record is specific. For example, write “Pickup address and weekday hours confirmed against the owner’s approved note of May 6.” A vague assertion such as “All details verified” is difficult for the client to use when something changes. Record what you checked, where the fact came from, and what you left for the client to decide. Keep the note short enough to maintain.

If the buyer wants multiple versions, include a shared source table. One policy line can feed a website, an email, and a sign. Build the table around the stable facts, then give each version a form appropriate to its audience. When a fact changes, update the shared record and trace it to each affected file. This is often more valuable than polishing one sentence in isolation.
Visual summary
Estimate the complete assignment
Agree on scope and revision limits
Deliver a usable approved version
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Confirm the approval record before publishing

Check that the final files match the version the client actually approved. A late correction can easily reach the editable document while an older PDF remains in the delivery folder. Compare the titles, dates, addresses, prices, and conditions across every promised format. Give the client a short list of what was delivered and identify any item still awaiting a decision. If you changed a file after approval, obtain an appropriate new confirmation rather than assuming that the earlier response covers new wording. This check belongs within your delivery effort and should be included in the time you estimate for future jobs.
Chapter 4 Compare a service with a downloadable product
Test whether a buyer can use the template independently.

Choose the offer where you can reach the buyer, verify the facts, and control the delivery. A small project you finish well gives you a sample and something concrete to improve. A buyer who says no can still tell you whether the problem is the audience, the price, or the work itself.
A studio preparation guide as a service

Take the photography preparation guide. A portrait studio wants clients to arrive with the right clothing options, have a place to park, and know which group members need to be present at the start. Interview the studio manager and ask for differences between outdoor and indoor sessions. Request the studio’s exact arrival window. Draft one basic guide and a clearly labeled set of notes for the second location.

Test it with a fictional customer who is bringing two children and traveling to the outdoor location. Can that person find where to meet the photographer and what to bring in under a minute? Ask the studio to approve the clothing guidance and any weather contingency. Deliver a printable page and a short email with a link to the complete guide. This is a small package the studio can use immediately and update between seasons.
Compare a service with a downloadable template

A service lets you charge for tailoring and checking facts. A downloadable template serves buyers who can complete those steps themselves. If three photographers tell you they need the same checklist with different arrival details, a template may be worth testing. Include sample entries, instructions, and obvious placeholders. Ask two studio owners to customize it while you observe. Rework the places where they hesitate before you spend money on a storefront or advertising.
Count the support a template needs

A downloadable product can be sold more than once, but each sale may still generate a question, a correction, or a request for help. Decide what the buyer receives and which help is included. If a template requires a skill the buyer may not possess, state that requirement before purchase. Give one completed fictional example and a short guide that explains how to replace its entries. A product becomes more useful when a buyer can recognize a successful result without contacting its author for every field.

Imagine a fictional studio checklist priced at twenty currency units. Ten sales produce two hundred units of revenue before fees, taxes, production, and support costs. They do not establish two hundred units of profit. If preparing and supporting those ten sales requires twelve hours, compare that actual effort with the service alternative. A reusable product may become more efficient with experience, but its first version can take longer than expected. Treat the calculation as a question to investigate, not a promise of passive income.
Visual summary
Compare service and product duties
Test the template with a buyer
Count production and support costs
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Choose a low-cost test before building a catalogue

Give two suitable test users the instructions and a fictional source brief. Ask them to complete the template without you explaining it aloud. Record where they hesitate and which entries they misunderstand. Fix those points before adding more designs. You can learn whether the product is usable with an ordinary document file and a clear sample; a paid storefront, advertising campaign, or subscription may not be needed for that first learning step.
Chapter 5 Turn a successful job into repeat work
Offer repeat work only where the client has a recurring need.

Recurring work makes sense when the buyer has recurring input. A weekly podcast produces an episode every week. A policy guide may need changes only when the owner updates the rules. Ask what changes, who supplies the information, and how quickly they need the new version.

Write a simple maintenance offer with an update frequency, boundaries, and one approval step. For example, “Every month I’ll revise up to five FAQ answers from one set of approved policy changes. Your manager will approve the revised answers before staff receives them.” Track how many requests really arrive before committing to a longer arrangement.

Keep a project record with the original promise, approved materials, delivery date, estimated and actual hours, and the buyer’s feedback. After three jobs, look for a concrete pattern. If customers pay promptly for intake forms and hesitate on social posts, interview one of each about how they made the decision. Improve your offer using what they tell you.

Close the week. Write one sentence describing a buyer you can reach, one task you can handle, and one date you will show them a sample. If your first offer drew little interest, use the next conversation to learn what people currently pay for. That information is progress you can use without another subscription or course.
Decide when to offer ongoing help

After delivering a set of customer replies to a repair shop, ask what has changed over the past three months. If the owner added a service or moved their drop-off area, a quarterly check may be sufficient. A weekly retainer would be difficult to justify unless there is weekly work. Write down who sends updates, when they are due, and how changes will be approved.

Give the buyer one simple measure they can understand. For the repair shop, the useful measure might be how often staff must ask for a missing item before creating a quote. Ask the client to track that for a small sample of requests before and after the changes. Note that staffing, season, and job mix may also affect the number. Use the feedback to improve the form instead of making a broad claim about results.
Recover when the first offer stalls

If prospects open the sample and never respond, ask one person whether the offer addresses a current need. If they find the sample useful but decline the scope, offer a smaller pilot with a clear endpoint. If they cannot supply reliable notes, choose a service with sources you can verify. Set a date to make that decision so the pitch does not drift for a month.

Review your progress using actions you control. Record the buyers interviewed, samples tested, paid offers made, and adjustments you tried. The first week may reveal a better question before it produces a paying customer. Take that question into the next conversation and use the answer to improve your offer.
Measure what changed and decide what to offer next

Start with a measure the customer can collect. A repair business could count how often an intake submission lacks an address or a preferred appointment window. A venue could record how many guests call for directions. A course instructor could watch whether learners can explain a mistake after reading the answer key. Agree on a short baseline and a comparable follow-up period when that is practical. Write down what else changed so you can describe the result responsibly.

If improvement is unclear, inspect the path a customer took rather than adding more words. The form may be accurate but hard to find. Staff may keep sending an older document. A second location may have different instructions. Fixing one detail in how the client uses the work may do more than creating a new deliverable. Ask the buyer which change would make the result easier to maintain. Decide whether maintenance is a good fit. An event venue may need new instructions whenever its entrance changes. A business with stable hours may need only an annual check. Offer continued help on the schedule actually supported by the work. Give the buyer a way to end the arrangement cleanly and retain the editable materials if that is part of your agreement.
Visual summary
Identify recurring inputs
Agree on update and approval duties
Review evidence before extending work
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
A seven day plan you can run with public or fictional material

On the first day, identify a business type and one result you can demonstrate. On the second day, assemble a fictional short example or use material you have permission to use. Spend the third day drafting the smallest useful version: one response, one worksheet, one form or one page. Give it a clear use case by naming the person who opens it and what they should be able to do.

On the fourth day, test it against an inconvenient case. Imagine the customer has no model number, the building entrance changed, or the supplier lists two conflicting measurements. On the fifth day, revise what the test exposed and write a short delivery note. On the sixth day, show the sample to an appropriate prospect or request feedback from someone who regularly does that work. Ask what part they would pay to avoid doing again.

On the seventh day, make a decision. Continue if the buyer can identify a specific benefit, you can find reliable source material, and the price accounts for verification and revisions. Change the offer if the problem is real but your sample solves the wrong part. Choose a different opportunity if the buyer rarely faces the problem or has an effective process already. Keep the best sample as evidence of how you work.
Chapter 6 Repair Intake and Product Comparisons
An intake form and a comparison sheet both depend on verified facts.
Opportunity 1 · A repair request that a technician can act on

A bicycle shop receives “my brakes are bad” through a general contact form. The technician must call to find out which brake, when the problem started, and whether the customer needs a pickup or can bring the bike in. Review three anonymized requests with the owner. Draft a form with separate fields for the customer’s description, the bike type and the preferred drop-off time. Leave diagnosis and the quote to the technician.

A shop owner pays for fewer incomplete requests and a clearer handoff to the service desk. Deliver a form, three fictional test submissions, and a one-page routing note. Ask ChatGPT to suggest plain-language field labels from the technician’s approved notes, then cut any field the shop cannot explain a reason for collecting. Use “I don’t know” where customers may lack technical details. A realistic request should reach staff even when the bike model is missing. Agree whether the quote covers wording only or also building the form in the shop’s software.
Pilot and quality check

Test a request from someone who does not know the bike model. If the form blocks them, allow an unknown option and provide a photo field only if the shop has approved how photos are collected. Deliver the form wording and a simple routing note for staff.
Practice with a sample · Repair intake

Compare these two fictional requests. “My bike clicks” identifies the symptom but gives no context. “The clicking starts when I pedal uphill, and the bike is available for drop-off Friday” gives staff a starting point. Set up your form so it can collect the second answer without expecting each rider to diagnose the source. Separate the requested date from a confirmed appointment. On delivery, give staff an example of what the completed form looks like and when they should call instead of emailing.
Opportunity 2 · A product comparison customers can trust

A cookware retailer wants a chart for three pans. Supplier sheets disagree about one pan’s induction compatibility. Prepare a chart with verified dimensions, weight, and care instructions. Mark the disputed compatibility claim for the owner to resolve before posting. Ask a reader to choose a pan for a small induction stove from the finished chart.

A store pays for helping customers choose among products without asking staff to interpret specifications. Deliver an editable comparison grid, a mobile-ready version, and a list of claim sources. Ask ChatGPT to map approved specs to rows and identify conflicting or missing values. Confirm those with the retailer before filling a cell. In the pilot, use three products and two reader tasks, such as finding the smallest induction-compatible pan and comparing handwashing requirements. Quote additional products separately if their data needs research.
Pilot and quality check

Deliver the chart plus its source sheet. When a supplier changes the model, the buyer can see exactly which cell needs reviewing. Ask the owner to approve wording about warranties, returns and availability.
Visual summary
Use verified source facts
Test the document’s next action
Keep technical judgment with the expert
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Practice with a sample · Product comparison

Create a separate verification sheet with one row for each claim. For a pan, record the applicable model number, the supplier document used, and when someone checked it. If the smaller model works on induction and the larger one is pending confirmation, show the verified fact for the smaller pan and leave the other claim for review. Ask ChatGPT to reorganize the sheet by what customers compare. Read across on a phone and ensure the first column stays understandable without scrolling.
Chapter 7 Business Emails and Podcast Packages
Review the business message and listen to the actual recording before delivery.
Opportunity 3 · An email that helps a buyer decide

A tile installer attends a home improvement show and receives permission from visitors to send project information. Draft a follow-up that explains the information needed for an estimate, such as approximate area, project location and timing. Include an example photo checklist instead of promising an exact quote from a picture.

An installer pays for a follow-up that produces useful information for an estimate. Deliver one email, one photo checklist and a reusable reply for people who do not yet have dimensions. Give ChatGPT the approved service area, the fields the installer needs, and the next step. Ask for a concise draft and a separate list of assumptions to confirm. Check that it tells readers where to send their information and who confirms the appointment. Measure the first small batch by how many useful replies it generates and which facts are still missing.
Pilot and quality check
Have the installer confirm who should receive the email and what the next step is. Test the message on a small screen and verify that the contact or scheduling link reaches the intended destination.
Practice with a sample · Estimate follow-up

Write a sample reply from a prospect who says only that they want tile in their kitchen. List the information a contractor can reasonably request before visiting. The work area, current surface, rough measurements, preferred timeline and permission to send photos may be useful. Ask the contractor which items are optional. If the information is insufficient for pricing, make the reply explain the next step. Send the test message to yourself and check whether your reply can be understood without opening the original thread.
Opportunity 4 · A podcast package with defensible timestamps

A podcast host wants notes for an episode about hiring a first employee. Use the authorized audio and transcript. Mark the moment each discussion actually begins, verify names against show notes and distinguish a guest’s opinions from factual claims. If the transcript mishears a name, check the audio and ask the host when needed.

A podcast producer pays for publishable material that makes a recording easier to navigate and promote. Agree on episode length, maximum number of markers, newsletter length and how to handle names the transcript cannot resolve. Ask ChatGPT for possible topics and a draft summary using an authorized transcript. Find timestamps yourself against the audio, then spot-check the markers in the publishing platform. For an initial package, work on a short segment and deliver one newsletter paragraph and three markers. Price longer episodes by actual editing and verification time.
Pilot and quality check

Deliver a short summary, timecoded chapter list and one newsletter excerpt. Play the audio around each marker. A listener should land at the start of the topic instead of hearing the previous speaker finish another point.
Visual summary
Preserve the client’s actual offer
Verify quotes and timestamps
Obtain approval before release
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Practice with a sample · Podcast package

Prepare a worksheet with columns for time, speaker, topic and a verification note. At a change of subject, mark where the new topic actually begins. If an automatic transcript groups two subjects into one paragraph, listen to the audio around the breakpoint. A host may want an excerpt about a useful tip while a first-time listener needs an episode summary. Deliver separate pieces for those jobs. Ask for feedback on each before deciding whether to bundle them in your next quote.
Chapter 8 Learning Exercises and Support Guides
A learner or staff member should be able to use the explanation in a real task.
Opportunity 5 · A practice exercise that teaches a decision

A spreadsheet instructor wants a worksheet on selecting the correct calculation for a sales report. Ask for one skill and one common error. Build a fictional dataset with one blank value and two unusually large orders. Have the learner choose a calculation and explain what the blank should mean before running it.

A course creator pays for a practice activity that shows whether learners can apply a lesson. Deliver a clean worksheet, a worked answer and a short note explaining a common mistake. Ask ChatGPT to propose two approaches a beginner might take and draft feedback for each. Run the calculation yourself, using the same spreadsheet setup as the learner. If a correct answer relies on something the course has yet to teach, change the exercise or add a prerequisite. Quote for a fixed number of exercises and specify who signs off on accuracy.
Pilot and quality check

Write an answer explanation showing how a different interpretation of the blank changes the result. Ask an instructor to check the calculation, then watch a learner use the worksheet. Revise the step where they first need help.
Practice with a sample · Spreadsheet lesson

Use a fictional sales sheet with five rows, one missing amount and one refund shown as a negative number. Ask the learner whether the goal is gross sales, net sales, or the average of completed orders. Then ask them to explain what counts as a completed order. Walk through the expected answer and one tempting wrong answer. Have ChatGPT suggest how to phrase feedback for that error, then confirm that the feedback directs the learner to the correct row or formula.
Opportunity 6 · A support guide that handles exceptions

A delivery business responds to refund requests with a paragraph copied from its policy. Staff still have to determine whether an item arrived damaged or was ordered by mistake. Build two short responses based on the approved policy and a handoff for claims that require a manager.

A service manager pays for support replies that reflect approved policy and tell staff when to escalate. Deliver a short reply library and a decision sheet tied to the actual returns process. With fictional tickets, ask ChatGPT for clear replies and have it mark facts it cannot infer. Review each proposed response with the policy owner. Test a damaged parcel, a normal return, and a request outside the stated window. Include a way for staff to identify the current version. A small pilot can cover one product line or one class of complaint.
Pilot and quality check

Test a scenario where the customer provides incomplete evidence. The reply should request only what the policy requires and avoid promising a refund before review. Confirm the language with the person who handles exceptions.
Visual summary
Define a usable learning outcome
Test routine and exception cases
Revise from observed questions
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Practice with a sample · Support replies

Build a simple scenario set covering a clear approval, a clear refusal under the approved policy, and a case staff must escalate. Ask the policy owner to explain the decision for each before you draft wording. In the escalation example, tell the customer which information staff needs and how they will hear back. Check that the sample avoids promising a particular resolution. Record who approves future edits. Staff should be able to tell the current response apart from a draft copied weeks earlier.
Chapter 9 Traffic Reports and Venue Arrival Guides
Compare the report with its data and test the arrival instructions with a new reader.
Opportunity 7 · A report that separates a pattern from a guess

A coffee shop wants to know why weekday traffic fell. It gives you sales totals and notes that it changed opening hours during the comparison period. Align the dates, compare equivalent opening hours and call out missing observations before writing a conclusion.

A business owner pays for a concise report that helps them decide what to investigate next. Deliver a chart, a data source note, and a paragraph separating observed changes from possible explanations. Use ChatGPT to propose comparisons, explain spreadsheet formulas, or draft chart captions from verified figures. Recompute the totals yourself and ask whether each week has the same operating hours. Demonstrate the result with fictional numbers before asking for access to internal records. Quote separately for cleaning data, making the report, and repeating it each month.
Pilot and quality check

Give the owner one chart and a short note listing what the records support. Identify one follow-up measurement, such as transactions per comparable open hour. Ask another person to recalculate one week from the same data.
Practice with a sample · Traffic report

If one week shows 180 transactions over 30 open hours and another shows 200 over 40 hours, compare the rates before calling the second week an improvement. The rates are six and five transactions per open hour. Those numbers still leave questions about the days covered and the types of customers who came in. Have ChatGPT draft a caption from the verified figures and explain the limitation in plain language. Ask the owner which one additional measurement would lead to a useful decision next week.
Opportunity 8 · Arrival instructions guests can actually use

An event venue has two doors and a different entrance for step-free access. Guests receive a street address but reach the wrong side of the building. Ask the coordinator to confirm usable entrances, parking, start time and a staffed contact point. Write arrival instructions in the order guests encounter them.

A venue pays for instructions that help first-time guests arrive without calling staff. Deliver a mobile email, a printable arrival sheet, and a short day-of reminder. Give ChatGPT approved address, parking, entrance and access details, then ask it to organize them in the order a guest will use them. Ask the venue to confirm details for the event date and test the directions with someone unfamiliar with the site. Scope an initial project to one venue and event. A second venue is a new fact-checking job even if the template carries over.
Pilot and quality check

Ask a person unfamiliar with the venue to read the directions and point out where they would go. Use their questions to improve the handoff. Ask the coordinator to confirm that the access details apply on the event date.

Opportunity 9 · A bilingual guide with a proper language review

A property manager needs move-in instructions in two languages. Collect approved instructions, identify building-specific terms and ask a qualified reviewer to resolve ambiguous wording. Keep keys, fees and access hours in a shared fact list so the two versions do not drift.

A property manager pays for usable move-in instructions in two languages. Deliver the source document, translated document and a shared approved fact list for access hours, keys and contact routes. Ask ChatGPT for a first pass or a list of ambiguous terms, then arrange a qualified language review. Price that review as part of the work. Have one reader of each version find the key pickup location and the after-hours contact without help. Label which version is approved and agree how policy updates will reach both languages.
Pilot and quality check

Ask a reader of each version to identify where to collect keys and whom to call after hours. Update the shared fact list before revising either version. Return both editable files and the review notes.
Practice with a sample · Bilingual move-in guide

Build a two-column checklist for the language reviewer. In the left column put the action a resident must take. In the right column record what both versions need to communicate, such as the location of key collection and the approved contact number. Have the reviewer flag a translation that sounds fluent but changes the action. Keep approved building names unchanged where the residents will see those names on doors and signs. Deliver a short note explaining which original facts need to be updated before either translation is revised.
Opportunity 10 · A handoff that works when automation fails

A design studio wants an automated reminder when an approval is late. Map who requests approval, who can approve, and when a reminder would be helpful. Test with fictional jobs, including an approved job and one where the due date changed.

A studio pays for fewer missed approvals and a clearer record of who owns the next action. Deliver a workflow map, a tested reminder prototype, and operating notes with a manual fallback. Ask ChatGPT to list acceptance tests from the approved approval sequence. Run the tests in a sample workspace with fictional jobs, including one that is complete and one with an extended deadline. Agree how staff will stop the reminder for canceled jobs. Price setup separately from monitoring or changes, and name who will own the workflow after handoff.
Pilot and quality check

Record how staff can check or send the reminder manually. Define what happens if the trigger runs twice, delivery fails or a project is canceled. Ask the studio to approve the workflow and its backup before using real client data.
